title: Cyrus and the Letters
premise: After a humiliating final concert ends his performing career, cellist Wendell Dunmore retreats to a fading seaside town and takes a job at the local library, where a community pen-pal program pairs anonymous writers. Through letters, he falls for a witty, wounded stranger — only to discover the correspondent is Marguerite Voss, the violinist whose rivalry and one cruel review helped end his career, and who is herself hiding that she is leaving for a permanent post in Vienna. As their written intimacy collides with their prickly real-world animosity, Wendell must decide whether love is worth another catastrophic performance. In the end, he plays again — not for critics, but for her — and asks her to miss the train.
about_author: Ines Montrose is a former orchestra librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's love letters donated to small-town archives. She writes from a drafty coastal cottage where the mail arrives late but always arrives.

chapters.title: The Broken String
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A flashback-tinged opening: the catastrophic final performance, the snapped string mid-solo, the silence afterward. Present-day Wendell unpacks in the seaside town, cello case unopened. Emotional beat: shame calcifying into a vow never to play again.

chapters.title: Dewey Decimal Heartache
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He starts at the Harrow Bay library under warm, meddling head librarian Mrs. Okonkwo, who treats him like an adopted nephew. She conscripts him into the annual anonymous pen-pal program. Beat: reluctant belonging beginning to take root.

chapters.title: Marguerite in Minor Key
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The celebrated violinist arrives in town to convalesce from burnout and a scandal of her own, renting the cottage next door. She recognizes Wendell instantly; he pretends not to know her. Beat: old wounds meeting new proximity.

chapters.title: Enemies, Apparently
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A disastrous encounter at the bakery — spilled coffee, barbed words about 'that review' — establishes open hostility. Mrs. Okonkwo witnesses it and, mischievously, assigns them each other as anonymous pen pals without telling either. Beat: comic friction masking attraction.

chapters.title: Dear Stranger
chapters.summary: Alternating POV via letters. Both write guarded first letters complaining about 'an insufferable neighbor.' Each finds the other's prose startlingly honest. Beat: the thrill of being seen without being known.

chapters.title: The Letters Get Braver
chapters.summary: Letters and scenes interleave. Pen-pals confess career griefs; in person, Wendell and Marguerite spar over the library's charity concert she's been roped into organizing. Beat: two relationships developing on parallel tracks, tension between them.

chapters.title: Salt and Rosin
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Walking the tideline at dusk, they share an almost-honest moment about why they stopped playing. She nearly tells him about Vienna; a phone call interrupts. Beat: longing sharpened by withheld truth.

chapters.title: Found Family, Found Trouble
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The library crew — Mrs. Okonkwo, teenage volunteer Priya, retired ferryman Gus — adopt both newcomers into a chaotic Sunday dinner. Wendell realizes he has a family again just as he fears losing it. Beat: warmth raising the stakes.

chapters.title: What the Letter Didn't Say
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Her pen-pal letter describing 'the man I wronged' lands in Wendell's hands; he reads it as fiction, moved, unaware it's about him. Meanwhile she accepts the Vienna contract by phone. Beat: dramatic irony tightening like a bowstring.

chapters.title: Duet, Unrehearsed
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Forced to substitute accompanying the children's choir, Wendell plays cello for the first time in a year — badly, then beautifully. Marguerite watches from the back row and weeps. Beat: the frozen thing inside him beginning to thaw.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. After the choir performance, adrenaline and rain push them into a kiss outside the library. Both pull back, terrified — she because of Vienna, he because of history. Beat: desire and dread in equal measure.

chapters.title: The Reviewer and the Reviewed
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Flashback chapter: years ago, under pressure from her mentor, she wrote the devastating review of Wendell's debut. Her guilt reframes everything. Beat: sympathy shifting toward her without excusing her.

chapters.title: Confession by Post
chapters.summary: Letters. Marguerite's pen-pal self confesses the review fully, naming no names but naming enough. Wendell, reading alone at night, matches details and realizes the truth: his stranger and his enemy are one. Beat: betrayal and tenderness colliding.

chapters.title: Cold Open
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He confronts her at the cottage; she admits everything except that she loves him. He walks out into the storm. Beat: the midpoint wound, deepest cut of the book.

chapters.title: Silence Between Movements
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Two weeks of silence. Priya and Gus stage interventions; Mrs. Okonkwo quietly gives Wendell Marguerite's final undelivered letter, which he refuses to read. Beat: grief performed as pride.

chapters.title: Packing Vienna
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Suitcases, a departure date ten days out, and a hollow victory. She plays alone in the empty church hall and understands she's running again. Beat: the cost of duty made concrete.

chapters.title: The Unread Letter
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. At 3 a.m. he finally opens her last letter: an apology, yes, but also the story of a girl taught that love was a liability, and a question — 'would you have stayed if I'd asked?' Beat: empathy breaking through anger.

chapters.title: One Last Train
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He learns the train time from Gus and makes a decision: not a grand speech, but a performance. He books the church hall, borrows the good piano tuner, and asks Priya to spread the word. Beat: resolve replacing retreat.

chapters.title: Cyrus Plays
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The concert: a program built around the piece that broke him, played whole this time before the whole found-family crowd. Midway, he dedicates a duet arrangement 'to M., who taught me the hard movements matter most.' Beat: catharsis through craft.

chapters.title: Platform Nine Minutes
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She hears of the concert too late, races from packing to station as the announcement calls her train. On the platform, torn between Vienna and Wendell, she hears, faintly, the town band — his encore — drifting down the hill. Beat: the choice compressed into minutes.

chapters.title: Stay After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. She runs up the hill, wet and furious and laughing, into the church where he is still playing. No speeches: she puts her violin case down beside his cello case and stays. They finally speak plainly — forgiveness asked and given. Beat: climax resolved in action, not argument.

chapters.title: Encore
chapters.summary: Epilogue, alternating. Spring: they decline Vienna together — or rather, defer it, choosing Harrow Bay and a teaching studio above the library. Final image: two instruments, one open window, letters still exchanged across the breakfast table. Beat: love chosen daily, duty renegotiated, home found.
